opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, that's a great question, and I think it's something I've reflected on quite a bit. Around 2015, 2016, computer vision was in a really interesting place. ImageNet had happened, deep learning had taken off, and recognition benchmarks were getting saturated pretty quickly. Classification, detection, even segmentation were working remarkably well. So a lot of people in the lab, including Fei-Fei and Silvio, started asking: what's the next frontier? What is vision actually *for*?

And the answer that kept coming back was that vision, in biological systems, isn't just about labeling pixels. It evolved to serve action. Animals see so they can move, grasp, avoid danger, interact with the world. So there was this growing feeling that if we want truly intelligent visual systems, we have to close the loop between perception and action. That's what people started calling embodied intelligence, or embodied AI.

There was also a practical side. Passive datasets have limits. You can collect millions of images, but the model never gets to poke at the world, see what happens, and learn from consequences. Robotics gives you that interactive learning signal. And at the same time, the tools were becoming available. Deep reinforcement learning was showing promising results, simulators were improving, and robot hardware was getting more accessible to academic labs.

For me personally, I found it very exciting because it turned a lot of vision problems into much harder and more meaningful ones. It's one thing to recognize a cup in an image. It's another to understand where to grasp it, how it'll move when you push it, and how that fits into a longer task like making a cup of tea. That's where you start needing reasoning, planning, and structure, not just pattern recognition. So the shift felt less like abandoning vision and more like asking vision to grow up and actually do something in the world.

r001.rationale: The candidate says vision benchmarks were saturating and the group began asking what the next frontier was, but it does not clearly say that the group felt computer vision had become less interesting.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. So, around 2016 and 2017, I was a PhD student at Stanford in Fei-Fei Li's lab, and if you remember that period, computer vision had just gone through this incredible run. ImageNet had basically been solved to the point where models were matching or beating humans on classification. Detection, segmentation, captioning — things were moving so fast that every few months a benchmark would fall.

And I think there was a shared feeling in the group, and honestly in a lot of the vision community, that we had been very good at building systems that look at the world and describe it, but they never had to act on what they saw. Perception was happening in a vacuum. You'd get a label, a bounding box, a caption, and then nothing. There was no consequence to being wrong beyond a number on a leaderboard.

Robotics felt like the natural place to close that loop. Fei-Fei had this framing that I found very compelling, which was that vision evolved in animals not so they could name things, but so they could move, find food, avoid danger. Perception and action co-evolved. So if we wanted to understand intelligence, or build it, we couldn't treat vision as a standalone module. We had to put it in a body and let it interact with the world.

There was also a practical dimension. Robot learning at the time was dominated by people coming from control and reinforcement learning, often with very low-dimensional state inputs and carefully instrumented setups. A lot of the perception-heavy ideas we had — learning from large-scale visual data, representation learning, imitation from video — hadn't really been brought over. So the group saw an opportunity to bring a vision-centric mindset into robotics, where the real question becomes: how do you learn useful behaviors from raw sensory input, and how do you scale that the way we scaled vision?

And for me personally, I just found it more honest as a research problem. When a robot fails to grasp a cup, there's no arguing with that. The world grades you. That accountability was very appealing after years of chasing benchmark numbers. It also turned out to be much harder than any of us expected, which I think is part of why I'm still working on it.

r001.rationale: The response describes a shared concern that vision systems only perceived and reported without acting, and says robotics offered a compelling next step. It does not clearly say the group felt computer vision had become less interesting.

astra-6.text:
I think the motivation was to go beyond perception. In computer vision, we were building systems that could recognize objects and understand scenes. But recognizing what’s in an image is only one part of intelligence. The next question is: can you use that understanding to do something in the world?

Robotics makes that question very concrete. If a robot needs to pick something up, it has to connect what it sees with how it moves, and then respond to what actually happens. That also changes what you need from vision—you need an understanding that supports action.

So I would describe it as a natural extension of computer vision. We wanted to study the connection between perception and action, and robotics gave us a way to bring those pieces together.

r001.rationale: The candidate describes robotics as a way to connect perception with action, but does not suggest that the group felt computer vision had become less interesting.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the motivation was to move from understanding the world to interacting with it. In computer vision, you might recognize objects or understand what’s happening in an image. But for a robot, that understanding has to support an action: what can I pick up, how should I move it, and what happens if I make a mistake?

That creates a different set of questions. Perception, learning, and control have to work together, and the robot’s actions change what it sees next. So the shift was really about taking the ideas we were developing in vision and asking how they could help an agent actually do something in the physical world.

r001.rationale: The response frames the shift as moving from visual understanding to physical interaction, but does not suggest the group felt computer vision had become less interesting.
